section_summary: This section documents mounting public pressure in late 1938 for the United States to halt exports of scrap iron, munitions, petroleum, and other strategic materials to Japan. It includes correspondence from churches, peace groups, academics, labor representatives, and Chinese relief advocates; a large California-Arizona petition; and State Department replies explaining the limits of the Neutrality Act and existing executive authority. The section concludes with a Shanghai consular report and the opening pages of the pamphlet “America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt,” which argues that American exports enabled Japan’s war in China.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of A. C. Johnson’s letters on amending the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Johnson’s December 12 letter enclosing two communications about amendment of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost confirms receipt of Johnson’s letter and its two enclosures concerning proposed changes to neutrality legislation. He thanks Johnson for supplying copies to the Department.

subfiles.title: Federal Council of Churches communication concerning war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Samuel McCrea Cavert
subfiles.about: A largely illegible incoming communication concerning proposals to prevent shipments of war raw materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR mainly preserves Federal Council of Churches letterhead, routing annotations, and the names of Cavert and Sayre. The date and subject are recoverable from Sayre’s reply on the following pages, which identifies it as Cavert’s November 25 letter about stopping shipments of raw materials of war to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Samuel McCrea Cavert concerning proposed restrictions on shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre
subfiles.about: Declines to endorse measures contemplated for a forthcoming Van Dusen article while urging careful assessment of their broader effects.
subfiles.summary: Sayre states his general support for practical efforts serving peace and American policy. He nevertheless declines to comment on the advisability of the specific measures Van Dusen planned to propose. He advises the Federal Council to weigh both immediate and remote effects and the broad interests of the American people.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting San Diego protest against scrap-iron shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Kate H. Dewing, Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom and San Diego Peace Committee
subfiles.about: Reports a San Diego mass meeting and petition demanding application of neutrality legislation and a ban on scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dewing describes a November 27 meeting in New Town Park held near 5,000 tons of scrap iron destined for Japan. Dr. Lewis B. Lesley’s motion asking Roosevelt to invoke neutrality legislation and place scrap iron on the banned list was unanimously approved. Dewing also reports that about 3,000 earlier petition signatures and another 1,000 signatures had been sent to the State Department.
keywords: Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Kate H. Dewing
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Dewing’s letters and additional petition signatures opposing exports of scrap iron and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Dewing’s November 19 and November 29 letters, including a petition and further signatures. Yost thanks her and refers her to earlier Department letters sent to Dr. W. J. Sherman and to Dewing herself. The response does not announce any new restriction on exports.

subfiles.title: Petition against shipment of scrap iron and war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Signatories assembled by the San Diego Peace Committee
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Petition sheets bearing signatures from San Diego, National City, Yuma, and other communities protesting exports of scrap iron and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The printed petition asks the President and Secretary of State to stop shipments of scrap iron and other war material to Japan. Dozens of sheets contain several hundred handwritten names and addresses, many heavily degraded by OCR, with concentrations in San Diego and National City and additional signatures from Arizona and other California communities. Several sheets are duplicate or overlapping reproductions, and page 101 records petition circulators.

subfiles.title: Request for a State Department interview and transmittal of an anti-export resolution
subfiles.from: Lillian B. Gilkes, West Side Committee to Aid China
subfiles.about: Requests an interview for I. F. G. Milner to present the committee’s views on U.S.-Japanese relations and encloses a resolution.
subfiles.summary: Gilkes says the committee represents people in more than thirty neighborhood churches and clubs. She asks that its representative, I. F. G. Milner, be received in Washington on December 9 or 10. The enclosed resolution expresses the committee’s opposition to continued American material support for Japan.
keywords: West Side Committee to Aid China

subfiles.title: Resolution urging prohibition of war-material exports to Japan and food assistance to China
subfiles.from: West Side Committee to Aid China meeting
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Calls for exports of war materials to Japan to be declared illegal and for surplus American food to be sold to China on credit.
subfiles.summary: The resolution condemns Japanese bombing of Chinese civilians, universities, and hospitals and argues that American scrap iron, petroleum, steel, aircraft, trucks, and other materials enable the destruction. It asks the President and Secretary of State to stop war-material shipments to Japan. It also urges aid to China through credit sales of surplus wheat and other foodstuffs.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lillian B. Gilkes explaining the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the existing Neutrality Act did not authorize the requested unilateral embargo and agrees to receive the committee’s representative.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential finding of war under the Neutrality Act would embargo arms, ammunition, and implements of war to both China and Japan, not Japan alone. He notes that the act does not cover other commodities and supplies license totals of roughly $14.3 million for China and $10.8 million for Japan since July 1937. The letter reiterates U.S. condemnation of civilian bombing and invites Milner to arrange a conference with R. V. Haig.

subfiles.title: Letter advocating use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act against Japan
subfiles.from: Lillian Barnard Gilkes, West Side Committee to Aid China
subfiles.about: Urges executive action under Section 338 of the Tariff Act to stop munitions and war materials from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gilkes explains that Milner was called back to New York and could not attend the planned interview. She argues that Section 338 provides a route for immediate executive action, especially given possible delay in revising the Neutrality Act. She encloses a resolution adopted by nearly two hundred people in upper Manhattan.
keywords: West Side Committee to Aid China

subfiles.title: Upper Manhattan resolution urging action under Section 338 and a boycott of Japanese goods
subfiles.from: Public meeting in upper Manhattan
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Demands use of Section 338 to block Japanese access to American war supplies and pledges a consumer boycott of Japanese goods.
subfiles.summary: The resolution describes Japan as a violator of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns bombing and discrimination against American interests in China. It argues that American oil, gasoline, scrap iron, trucks, and machinery sustain the Japanese war effort. The meeting urges immediate action under the Tariff Act and pledges not to buy Japanese goods while the aggression continues.

subfiles.title: Reply rejecting use of Section 338 to restrain exports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that Section 338 governs imports into the United States and cannot be used to prohibit exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Gilkes’s letter and the December 13 resolution. He states that Section 338 authorizes restrictions on imports from foreign countries under specified conditions but gives no authority to restrain American exports. He refers Gilkes back to the Department’s December 7 explanation of the Neutrality Act.

subfiles.title: Arthur A. Holcombe letter supporting stronger action on munitions exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Arthur A. Holcombe
subfiles.about: Endorses stronger action to halt American munitions supplies to Japan and broader executive discretion under neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Holcombe reports receiving an appeal from Harry B. Price for telegrams and letters supporting more vigorous action. Rather than join the mass campaign, he writes directly to Hornbeck so his views can be used in gauging public opinion. He favors giving the executive wider discretion under the Neutrality Act and authorizes use of his name.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledgment to Arthur A. Holcombe
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Records Holcombe’s support for stronger restrictions and for greater executive discretion under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck summarizes the essential points of Holcombe’s December 6 letter. He notes Holcombe’s desire for stronger action against munitions supplies to Japan and his willingness to have his name used in support of broader executive discretion.

subfiles.title: ILWU telegram concerning picketing of the M.S. Pyros
subfiles.from: Germain Bulcke, president, ILWU Local 1-10
subfiles.about: Warns that mass picketing of a scrap-iron ship in San Francisco could cause a coastwide port shutdown and asks for an embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bulcke reports that as many as 2,000 Chinese men, women, children, and supporters were preventing longshoremen from loading the M.S. Pyros, chartered by Mitsui to carry scrap iron to Japan. Waterfront employers were threatening to close the port. He asks Hull for immediate action and a wire stating the Department’s position.

subfiles.title: State Department telegram to Germain Bulcke
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: States that existing law provides no authority to restrict scrap-iron exports and that new legislation is a matter for Congress.
subfiles.summary: The reply directly addresses Bulcke’s December 19 telegram. It says no existing legal authority permits prohibition or restriction of scrap-iron exports to any foreign country. The Department places responsibility for any such measure with Congress.

subfiles.title: White House referral of B. S. Fong’s telegram
subfiles.from: M. H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers B. S. Fong’s telegram to the State Department for consideration and acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: The White House sends the telegram to the Department without substantive comment. It asks the Department to consider and acknowledge the appeal, which concerned the San Francisco picketing of a Japan-bound scrap-iron vessel.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to B. S. Fong on scrap-iron exports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.to: B. S. Fong, China War Relief Association
subfiles.about: Explains why neither the Neutrality Act nor another existing statute authorized the President to stop scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Fong’s report that about 2,000 people were picketing a Japan-bound scrap-iron ship in San Francisco. He explains that a Neutrality Act proclamation would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan, while scrap iron was not among the enumerated arms and implements of war. The letter states that no existing statute authorized a scrap-iron embargo and supplies comparative arms-export license totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Circulation of Propaganda Against American Assistance in Japan’s War on China
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Reports the Shanghai reprinting and distribution of “America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt” and related form letters.
subfiles.summary: Gauss submits a Shanghai reprint of a New York pamphlet opposing American assistance to Japan, together with an envelope containing advocacy letters and a “Summary of Peace Act.” The materials encourage Americans to urge government officials to halt munitions, raw materials, supplies, and credits to Japan. The Consulate attributes the local printing to missionaries M. O. Williams and R. L. Paty and notes that copies were also sent to the embassies in Beijing, Chongqing, and Tokyo.
keywords: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt

subfiles.title: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: American public, including Americans in China
subfiles.about: Argues that American exports sustained Japanese aggression in China and calls for economic non-participation and an embargo on war supplies.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet contends that Japan depended heavily on American iron, steel, petroleum, copper, aircraft, trucks, and machinery and that withholding those materials could shorten the war. It presents economic data, press reports, and statements by Henry Stimson, Roosevelt, Hull, Sayre, Hornbeck, and members of Congress to support sanctions or an embargo. Tables compare national contributions to Japanese strategic imports, while quoted legislators condemn attacks on civilians and alleged violations of the Nine-Power Treaty. The pamphlet continues beyond page 160.
keywords: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt
